job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Lena Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the graduate scheme at Harbourside Savings Bank in Plymouth. I rotate through teams every six months, and right now I'm in customer operations, handling account queries and small business loans. I started in September. I rent a flat above a bakery with my sister's old school friend, and I run the youth group at our church on Thursday evenings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moments when someone who's anxious about money leaves feeling lighter, like the woman who thought she'd lost her late husband's account. The hard part is the targets, because we get a daily number of cases and nobody asks how hard they were. My parents run a small cafe, Reyes Kitchen, and they've told me they'd back me if I ever wanted to do my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I'd rather people were calm about it. At work I'd say the tools help me with the paperwork, and the real work is still with the customer. I'd tell my youth group that useful things last and hype doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, and I get quicker at it. Harbourside is stable, Plymouth has banks and building societies, and I have over six months saved. I'd also still get to rotate, which is how I find out what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the scheme, finish my banking exams and keep learning the AI tools, since I enjoy them. I'd save about £500 a month, and put a little into my parents' cafe if they need it. And I'd keep leading the youth group, because that's what I love most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the picture where I can plan things, like a holiday, without checking the news first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day. What do they do for you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for summarising long customer histories, drafting letters in plain words and checking my sums. The tools save me an hour a day, which I spend on the phone with the customers who need patience. I like that bit, so it's a good trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cafe, a bit. Margins are thin, and my parents work six days a week. If food prices keep climbing, my dad says he might have to cut a staff member. I'd quietly worry about that, whether or not AI did anything.

say: I'd say good, I'd rather people were **calm** about it.
I'd tell my youth group that **useful things** last and hype doesn't.
think: I keep my job and get **quicker** at it, and Harbourside is stable.
Plymouth has banks and building societies, and I have **savings**.
do: Carry on with the **graduate scheme** and finish my banking exams.
Save about **£500 a month**, with a little for my parents' cafe if needed.
Keep leading the **youth group** on Thursdays.
feel: I feel **calm**, as I can plan a holiday without checking the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving, so let's be sensible. I'd tell my manager that the bank should train us and keep us in customer work, since that's where trust is. And I'd tell my youth group that learning never wastes anyone's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the question-answering, the checking and the standard loans are on the card. Customer operations is exactly the work a tool can do, like answering a balance query or filling a loan form. So Harbourside will need fewer of us on the floor. But I'm good with the tools, and I think that counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use my next rotation to move into relationship banking or small business lending, where the customer needs a person. I'd learn the tools more deeply, maybe even build a helper for the team. I'd also save £700 a month and talk to my parents about the cafe, because small businesses are what I'd like to serve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but eager. I know change is coming and I'd rather meet it than hide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your rotation are on the card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The balance queries, the simple loans and the letters. The calls where someone's frightened, or the shop owner who's trying to save their business, stay with people for longer. I want to be in those conversations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every generation's work changes, and the things that stay are honesty and kindness. That's what I'd tell my youth group. I'd say learn the new things, but don't lose the old. I'd also say be someone people trust, because that's the one thing no tool can hand out.

say: I'd say it's moving, so let's be **sensible** and train people.
I'd tell my youth group that learning **never wastes** anyone's time.
think: The **standard** loans and queries are on the card, so Harbourside needs fewer on the floor.
I'm good with the **tools**, and that should count for something.
do: Use my next rotation to move into **relationship banking** or small business lending.
Learn the tools more **deeply** and maybe build a helper for the team.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but eager, since I'd rather meet change than hide.

fieldNote: Lena treats her scheme as a **chance** to rotate toward trust-based roles.
She uses **youth group** language to frame the change as ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and ordinary families will pay for it. I'd say churches and communities have to be ready to look after people, and firms should keep their staff. I'd say it to my youth group gently, because they're worried about exams and jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the bank job as I know it goes in 2028. Banking is thinking work, and a machine that can do it better and cheaper will take most of it. The robots three years later don't touch my desk. I'd be twenty-four with a degree and a lot of questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd pray, then I'd make a spreadsheet of my money, which is over six months. I'd save £900 a month and cut the extras. I'd ask my parents if I could help in the cafe on weekends, because a cafe has a lot of hands-on work, and that lasts longer. And I'd look for work where a human has to be there, like care or community banking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit sad. I'd have to explain to my youth group why a degree might not protect them. That would hurt more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years leaves very little time. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cafe is hands-on, so it should last longer than my desk. That might make it safer, and I'd happily help there. But a cafe depends on customers having money, and if lots of people lose jobs, they stop eating out. So I'd worry for them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your parents' cafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use my AI skills for something useful, like helping my parents with their ordering and books, so they can keep going. I'd rather be useful than panicky. It's a small step, but it's mine to take.

say: I'd say ordinary families will **pay** for this, and firms should keep their staff.
I'd say churches and communities must be ready to **look after** people.
think: Privately, the bank job as I know it **goes in 2028**.
The robots come later and don't touch my **desk**, so there's no extra time.
do: Make a **spreadsheet** of my money and save £900 a month.
Offer to help at the **cafe** on weekends.
Look for work where a **human** has to be there, like care or community banking.
feel: I feel **anxious** and sad, especially for my youth group.
S2.quote: A cafe depends on customers having money, and if lots of people lose jobs, they stop eating out.
fieldNote: Lena sees the cafe as **hands-on** but dependent on spending power.
Her first move is practical: money **spreadsheet**, then family help.
She feels more for her **youth group** than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's prepare people instead of panicking. I'd say employers and churches should run training, and families should be ready to help. I'd say it to the whole youth group, because they're the ones who'll face it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have a few years of work, and by 2031 I'd be twenty-seven, possibly with a family. I'd expect the bank role to shrink a lot by then, but I'd have time to do something else, probably involving small businesses. I feel more settled than with two years, but I'm not complacent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the banking exams in two years, then move into small business lending. I'd learn the AI tools to a high level, so I could help my parents' cafe and other small shops. And I'd save £700 a month and think about opening a small bookkeeping and advice service for cafes and shops on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. I'm a bit nervous and a bit excited, like before a big trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you a bit more room. What would you do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents first, because they've run a business through bad years. Then the bank's senior people about where roles are going. And I'd talk to my pastor, because it helps to have someone who's wise and calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The five-year one lets me build my own plan. In the two-year one I'm reacting. Here I can aim at something, like helping local shops with their money, and put my skills toward it.

I'd say employers and churches should run **training**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and we should use it well. I'd say the church, schools and employers should all do their part. I'd say it cheerfully, because I do think we can get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. By 2036 I'd be thirty-two, probably married, maybe with a child, and running something of my own. I'd have changed my work two or three times, and that wouldn't frighten me, because I'm used to learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my bank job a few years, then move into small business advice. I'd save for a house with my future husband, and put a bit toward my parents' cafe if they need it. I'd keep leading the youth group and try the AI tools on everything. And I'd teach other people how to use them, because that's the best way to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and cheerful. It feels like a road I can walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does ten years mean for your life plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them they've built something good, and they can keep it going with some help. I'd say let me help with the books and the ordering, so you can spend time with customers. And I'd say they don't have to do this alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to open a small advice service for local businesses, with a bit of tech and a lot of people. I'd also want a family and a home in Plymouth. I think ten years is enough to have both, if I look after my money and my relationships.

I'd say it **cheerfully**, because I think we can get through it.
think: For me it's **fine**, and by 2036 I'd be thirty-two, perhaps married.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would put a lot of people under pressure at once, including my parents' customers. What would help is firms and the government being honest early, retraining that leads to real work, and communities like my church looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I feel fortunate, and I want to use it to help others. I have savings, a family who'd catch me, and these tools I use every day. If I can help a few people through it, that's what I'd like to do.
